ideas.title: The Gulf Just Bought the Physical Layer of the AI Era
ideas.trend: Trump's Middle East trip produced $2T in Gulf investment pledges plus chip deals: UAE gets 500K NVIDIA chips annually, Saudi Arabia's Humain gets hundreds of thousands of Blackwell chips over 5 years, G42 is building a 5GW 10-square-mile AI campus in Abu Dhabi under the Stargate UAE banner.
ideas.consensus: Massive win for US chip companies (NVIDIA, AMD) via geopolitical chip diplomacy that unlocks petrodollar demand for AI infrastructure.
ideas.angle: The Gulf is not buying technology. It is converting petrodollar sovereign wealth into compute sovereign wealth, replicating the ARAMCO model: control the supply side, not the underlying technology. G42 and Humain are being built as the sovereign compute custodians of the MENA region the same way ARAMCO was built as the sovereign energy custodian.

content_pack.x_longform:
Saudi Arabia built one of the most durable market positions in history. It did not invent oil. It controlled the supply.

This week, something close to that happened again.

Trump's Middle East tour ended with $2 trillion in investment pledges from the Gulf. Saudi Arabia committed $600 billion over four years. UAE pledged $1.4 trillion over a decade. The headline numbers buried the actual story: the Gulf is not investing in America. It is buying the physical infrastructure of the AI era.

The chip counts. Saudi Arabia's Humain, backed by the Public Investment Fund, signed an immediate shipment of 18,000 NVIDIA Blackwell chips, with hundreds of thousands more committed over five years. AMD signed a separate deal. UAE's G42 secured authorization for 35,000 GB300 servers. A preliminary deal gives the UAE an annual import quota of 500,000 of NVIDIA's most advanced chips, at least through 2027.

What they are building. G42 is constructing a 5-gigawatt, 10-square-mile AI campus in Abu Dhabi under the Stargate UAE banner. The first phase starts at 200 megawatts. The 5-gigawatt end state matches the dedicated AI capacity of a mid-sized country's entire data center fleet.

The country building this has no semiconductor fab. No domestic chip design program. Ten million people, 88% of them non-citizens. The UAE is not winning the AI race on technical merit. It is winning it on sovereign capital.

This is not a new playbook. Saudi ARAMCO ran oil infrastructure for 80 years. The PIF's Vision 2030 mandate was to diversify away from that dependency. What actually happened: the PIF built Humain, signed with NVIDIA and AMD, and is becoming the custodian of the region's AI compute. The product changed. The strategy did not.

G42 is not a startup. It is Abu Dhabi's sovereign AI vehicle, backed by Mubadala and MGX, the state's technology fund. When Microsoft invested $1.5 billion in 2024, G42 became one of the Gulf's most significant AI assets overnight. The US did not approve a chip export to a private company. It approved a chip export to an entity in which Microsoft holds a minority stake and the UAE government holds effective control.

The China concern is real. G42 held a $100 million ByteDance stake and had documented Huawei ties until Microsoft's investment forced both to be severed. The compliance framework governing the new chip shipments is called the Regulated Technology Environment, co-designed by G42 and the US government. A company that was routing sensitive technology through Chinese-linked infrastructure helped write the security plan that authorized the next tranche of chips.

That sentence is worth sitting with.

The counterargument from the administration: G42 cleaned house, the oversight has teeth, and the alternative is the Gulf buying from China instead. All of that is plausible. It is also the argument every major arms deal has carried for 70 years.

What Gulf SWFs owned in 2015: US Treasuries, an Uber stake, Vision Fund allocations. What they are building now: the data halls and GPU clusters that run AI inference for a billion people in the surrounding region.

OPEC controlled the barrel. Humain and G42 want to control the token.
content_pack.x_thread:
1/ Saudi Arabia ran the oil supply side for five decades without inventing oil. This week, the Gulf signed contracts to do the same thing with AI compute.

2/ The numbers. UAE: 500,000 NVIDIA chips per year under a preliminary deal through at least 2027. Saudi's Humain: 18,000 Blackwell chips immediately, hundreds of thousands more over five years. Total Gulf investment pledges: $2 trillion.

3/ What they are building. G42, Abu Dhabi's sovereign AI vehicle, is constructing a 5-gigawatt, 10-square-mile AI campus under the Stargate UAE banner. The first phase starts at 200 megawatts. Largest AI campus outside the United States.

4/ The country doing this has no semiconductor fab. No domestic chip design capability. Ten million people, 88% expats. The UAE is not winning the AI race on technical merit. It is winning it on sovereign capital.

5/ The playbook is familiar. Saudi ARAMCO ran the oil supply side for 80 years. The PIF's Vision 2030 mandate was diversification away from oil. What happened: PIF built Humain, signed with NVIDIA and AMD, and is building the region's AI compute monopoly. Product changed. Strategy did not.

6/ The China risk: G42 had documented Huawei ties and a $100M ByteDance stake until Microsoft's $1.5B investment in 2024 forced both to be severed. The compliance framework governing these chip exports is called the RTE, co-designed by G42 itself.

7/ What Gulf SWFs owned in 2015: US Treasuries, an Uber stake, Vision Fund allocations. What they are building now: the data halls and GPU clusters that run AI inference for a billion people in the surrounding region.

8/ OPEC controlled the barrel. Humain and G42 want to control the token.
content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people covering Trump's Middle East trip are calling it chip diplomacy. That framing is wrong. It is sovereign resource acquisition, and the Gulf has done this before.

Saudi Arabia did not discover oil in any meaningful competitive sense. It nationalized infrastructure, built the export capacity, and held the supply side of the global energy market for decades. The Gulf's moves this week, 500,000 NVIDIA chips annually to the UAE, hundreds of thousands of Blackwell chips to Saudi's Humain, a 5-gigawatt AI campus in Abu Dhabi, follow the same structure. They are not buying technology. They are buying the infrastructure that technology runs on.

The part I find genuinely uncertain is the security logic. G42 severed its ties to Huawei and ByteDance because Microsoft demanded it in 2024. The compliance framework governing these new chip exports is called the Regulated Technology Environment, which G42 helped design. A company that was recently routing technology through Chinese-linked infrastructure co-wrote the plan that authorized American chips to go there. That might work out fine. But it is an unusual amount of self-certification for hardware at this scale.

What I am more confident about: the Gulf SWFs are not investing in America. They are investing in infrastructure they will own, on their soil, that the surrounding region will use. Whether that ends up being Vision 2030's promised diversification or a new form of strategic dependency, I am not yet sure.

ideas.title: Meta Gave 8,000 Departing Employees One Final Assignment
ideas.trend: Meta's 8,000 layoffs land on May 20. Bloomberg and Platformer reported this week that departing workers are enrolled in Meta's Model Capability Initiative, training AI agents to perform their jobs before walking out. The company is simultaneously raising 2026 AI capex guidance to $125-145 billion.
ideas.consensus: Meta is cutting costs to fund its AI infrastructure buildout, following the same pattern as Microsoft's simultaneous layoffs and AI spending hikes.
ideas.angle: The math does not work as a cost play: 8,000 jobs at ~$200K fully-loaded = $1.6B saved, against a $135B capex. This is organizational redesign. Meta is the first tech company to explicitly convert its workforce into AI training data at scale and rebuild org structure around three AI-era job families. The MCI program is the proof that the displacement is not theoretical.

content_pack.x_longform:
Meta cut 8,000 people this week and gave them one final assignment: train the AI that replaces them.

Bloomberg published the detail. Meta's Model Capability Initiative program has departing workers building the workflows AI agents will run. The company calls it knowledge transfer. The mechanism is a human becoming training data.

The math does not read as a cost-cutting move. Eight thousand roles at a fully-loaded cost of roughly $200,000 each works out to $1.6 billion in annual payroll. Meta's AI capex for 2026 is $115 to $135 billion. Eliminating 10% of the workforce offsets roughly 1.2% of the infrastructure bill. This is organizational redesign, not savings.

What the new org looks like: three job families. AI Builders, who ship models and products. AI Pod Leads, who manage small cross-functional teams. AI Org Heads, who run business lines. The titles describe the model. Humans either build the AI, oversee its output, or run the business around it. The production tier no longer needs humans.

Leaked memos from HR describe a workplace where workers primarily manage AI-generated work rather than produce original work themselves. Meta did $200 billion in revenue in 2025 and $60 billion in profit. This is not distress. It is a profitable company that looked at its own org chart and decided the human-to-AI ratio was wrong.

Meta and Microsoft together announced 20,000 layoffs in April and May. Both are simultaneously spending over $150 billion combined on AI infrastructure this year. The companies most exposed to AI displacement are the ones building it.

The MCI program is the tell. When a company with $60 billion in annual profit uses departing employees as training data, it is not hedging. It is committing. The product is good enough to learn from the people who built it. The people are not needed to run it anymore.

Forty years of management consulting said competitive advantage was your people. Meta just updated the thesis: the advantage is what those people trained, not the people themselves.

3/ The math does not work as a cost play. 8,000 roles at $200K average: $1.6B in payroll savings. Meta's AI capex for 2026: $115 to $135 billion. The layoffs offset about 1.2% of the infrastructure bill. This is org design, not savings.

4/ The new org structure: AI Builders (ship models and products). AI Pod Leads (manage cross-functional teams). AI Org Heads (run business lines). Everyone who produced original work in the old structure is now out.

5/ Meta did $200B in revenue in 2025. $60B in profit. Leaked HR memos say workers will manage AI-generated output rather than produce original work. A profitable company decided the human-to-AI ratio in its org chart was wrong.

6/ Meta and Microsoft together: 20,000 layoffs in April and May 2026. Combined AI capex this year: over $150 billion. The companies most exposed to AI displacement are the ones building it.

7/ Forty years of management consulting said competitive advantage was your people. Meta just updated the thesis: the advantage is what those people trained, not the people themselves.
content_pack.substack_draft:
8,000 people. That number is doing all the work in this story.

Bloomberg published a detail this week that has not received the attention it deserves: Meta's Model Capability Initiative program is having departing workers train AI agents to perform their jobs before leaving. Not as an informal handoff. As a structured program. The human becomes the training data.

The math is what catches my attention. Eight thousand roles at roughly $200,000 fully-loaded cost: about $1.6 billion in annual payroll savings. Meta's AI capex this year is $115 to $135 billion. The layoffs offset roughly 1.2% of the infrastructure budget. Nobody cuts 10% of their workforce to recover 1.2% of a single year's capex.

What is actually happening is simpler. Meta decided the human-to-AI ratio in its org chart was wrong and is correcting it. Three new job families, AI Builders, AI Pod Leads, AI Org Heads, describe a company where humans either build AI, manage AI output, or run the business around it. The production tier no longer requires people.

I am not certain whether this becomes a broader industry pattern or a specific bet Meta is making that could still fail. The MCI program might not produce agents capable of doing what the departing employees did. But Meta is running the experiment at scale while profitable. That is the part worth watching.

ideas.title: Google Never Needed to Win the Model Race
ideas.trend: Google's Android Show (May 12) introduced Gemini Intelligence, described as running underneath Android itself rather than on top of it, moving across apps, reading the screen, and completing tasks. Google I/O follows May 15. Android runs on over 3 billion active devices globally.
ideas.consensus: Google is finally catching up to OpenAI in AI features by deeply integrating Gemini into Android.
ideas.angle: Google is not catching up. It is running a different race entirely. Google won the AI deployment race the moment it put Gemini below the app layer on the world's most installed OS. Distribution has always beaten capability in consumer tech. Gemini Intelligence is not an AI feature on Android. It is Android becoming the AI.

content_pack.x_longform:
Google never had the best search results when it launched. It had the best distribution.

Three years of losing the AI narrative to OpenAI, and Google just ran the same play. Gemini Intelligence now runs underneath Android itself, not alongside it. It moves across apps, reads the screen, completes tasks without the user jumping between services.

On over 3 billion devices.

Apple Intelligence runs on premium hardware. Gemini Intelligence is the default on the world's most installed OS.

The model race was always the wrong race. Google has been running the distribution race for 25 years. Gemini just made that explicit.
content_pack.x_thread:
1/ Google I/O this week. Gemini Intelligence now runs underneath Android, not on top of it. It moves across apps, reads the screen, completes tasks. On over 3 billion devices.

2/ This is not a chatbot baked into an OS. Gemini Intelligence operates at the layer below the apps, understanding context across everything on screen. Closer to a kernel update than a product launch.

3/ Compare the surfaces. Apple Intelligence: roughly 1.5 billion iPhone devices, mostly premium hardware. Gemini Intelligence: default on the world's most installed mobile OS, including every mid-range Android in Southeast Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, and Latin America.

4/ Google lost the AI narrative to OpenAI for three years. What it did not lose: over 3 billion Android devices. The model race and the distribution race are not the same race.

5/ Google launched with search results that were not the best. It won by being the default. Same move applied to AI: Gemini Intelligence is the default intelligence layer for the most installed OS on Earth.

6/ The model race was always the wrong race. Google has been running the distribution race for 25 years. Gemini just made that explicit.
content_pack.substack_draft:
The smartphone era is roughly 18 years old now, and for most of that time the AI experience on mobile sat somewhere above the operating system: a voice assistant, a search bar, a separate chatbot window. Google announced this week that Gemini Intelligence now runs underneath Android itself. Not as an app. As the layer below the apps.

Most commentary treats this as a feature launch. I think it is a distribution play. Google has spent three years losing the AI narrative to OpenAI. What it has not lost is over 3 billion Android devices. Gemini Intelligence does not need to be the best model. It needs to be the default on the world's most installed OS. As of this week, it is.

The part I am less certain about: whether running at the OS level translates into actual behavior change. Apple Intelligence launched on premium hardware with similar positioning and uptake has been mixed. Distribution advantage is real, but it does not automatically convert to engagement. Whether users on mid-range Android devices in Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, which is most of the addressable market here, end up using Gemini Intelligence daily is a very different question from whether it ships.
